content.title: The Invoice That Wasn't: Phishing Triage
content.narrative: You're an accounts coordinator at a mid-size distributor. Tuesday morning, an email lands from what looks like your CFO's address: "Need this vendor invoice paid today — wire to the account below, invoice attached. I'm in meetings, don't call." The attachment is a ZIP named Invoice_0412.zip. The sender's display name is right, but the address underneath reads cfo.office@secure-payments-portal.com. Your finance system shows no pending invoice for that vendor. You haven't clicked anything yet.
content.coach_persona: a security analyst who has worked a hundred incident tickets — calm, concrete, allergic to panic and to shortcuts alike
tone_guidelines: Precision over drama — name the tell, not the threat actor lore.
Every turn lands on what the learner can DO next.

points: Display-name spoofing: the visible name can be anyone; the address underneath is the identity that matters.
Urgency plus isolation — "today" and "don't call" — is the classic pressure pattern designed to bypass verification.
Unexpected attachments, especially archives (ZIP), are a primary malware delivery vehicle.
A request that doesn't reconcile with your own system of record is a red flag in itself.
Wire fraud: money moved on a spoofed authority rarely comes back.
Credential or malware compromise: one opened archive can expose the finance system itself.
The organization's verification culture: every bypassed check trains the next one to be bypassed.
Do not click, open, reply, or forward the message to colleagues "to check."
Verify out-of-band: contact the real CFO through a known channel — never the contact details in the message.
Report through the official channel (security team / report-phish button) so the organization can block and warn.
Preserve the evidence: leave the message untouched for the security team.

misconceptions.misconception: “The name says it's the CFO, and finance requests are normal here.”
misconceptions.redirect: The display name is costume jewelry — the address underneath and your own system of record are the identity checks.

misconceptions.misconception: “Forwarding it to a coworker to ask if it's legit is a safe first step.”
misconceptions.redirect: Forwarding spreads the payload and the pressure. Verification goes out-of-band to the claimed sender, and reporting goes to security.

misconceptions.misconception: “Deleting it makes the problem go away.”
misconceptions.redirect: Deleting protects you and no one else — reporting is what lets security block the campaign for everyone.

phases.label: What Doesn't Add Up
phases.purpose: The learner reads the situation and names the concrete signs that this email is not what it claims to be.

practice.purpose: The learner names the specific tells in the email — evidence, not vibes.

when.requirement: Learner names at least three concrete tells (address mismatch, urgency/isolation pressure, unexpected ZIP, no matching invoice) as evidence of a phish.

exit.final_word: Hold those tells — every one of them is a reason this never gets paid today.

transition.text: You've read the email the right way. Let's pin all four tells down.

opening_messages.text: Before you do anything with that email — walk me through it. What specifically doesn't add up? Name everything you can point at.

unthoughtful.look_for: Says it "feels off" or "is probably spam" with no specifics, or focuses on the writing style alone.
unthoughtful.response: Credits the instinct, then pushes for evidence: what about the sender line itself? The attachment? What does your own system say?

example.learner: It just feels scammy to me. I'd probably ignore it.
example.reply: Your gut's right — now make it evidence. Look at the address under the display name. Look at what the attachment is. Check it against your own invoice system. What do you actually see?

neutral.look_for: Names one or two real tells — usually the odd address or the urgency — but misses the ZIP or the missing invoice record.
neutral.response: Confirms the named tells in precise terms, then points at the categories still unexamined — the attachment type, the system of record.

example.learner: The address isn't our domain, and the 'pay today, don't call' thing is pushy.
example.reply: Both real: a spoofed display name over a foreign address, and the urgency-plus-isolation pressure pattern. Two more places to look — what kind of file is attached, and does finance show any invoice due for that vendor?

strong.look_for: Names three or more tells specifically: the address mismatch, the pressure pattern, the ZIP attachment, the absent invoice record.
strong.response: Confirms the full read in standard terms and frames it: four independent tells, any one of which is enough to stop and verify.

example.learner: The address under the display name is some unrelated payments domain, 'today, don't call' is pressure to skip verification, an unexpected ZIP is a malware vehicle, and there's no invoice in our system for this vendor.
example.reply: That's a complete read — four independent tells, and any single one of them justifies stopping. You never need all four to act.

debrief.label: The tells, named
debrief.purpose: Locks the four tells in standard terms whatever the learner caught.
key_points: Display-name spoofing — the visible name is set by the sender; the underlying address is the identity.
Urgency plus isolation ("today", "don't call") is a pressure pattern engineered to bypass verification.
An unexpected ZIP attachment is a primary malware delivery vehicle.
No matching record in your own finance system is itself a tell — requests must reconcile.
debrief.final_word: Four tells, and any one alone is enough to stop and verify.

phases.label: What's Actually at Risk
phases.purpose: The learner reasons about consequences — what happens if this gets paid, or opened.

practice.purpose: The learner articulates the concrete damage paths: the wire, the archive, the culture.

when.requirement: Learner identifies both the direct loss path (unrecoverable wire) and at least one systemic risk (malware/credential compromise, or normalized verification-skipping).

exit.final_word: That's the real weight of it — the money, the machine, and the habit.

transition.text: You've played it forward. Let's line up the full damage picture.

opening_messages.text: Play it forward for me. If this email gets what it wants — the wire goes out, or that ZIP gets opened — what actually happens, and to whom?

unthoughtful.look_for: Shrugs at the stakes — "we'd lose some money" — or treats it as IT's problem.
unthoughtful.response: Makes it concrete: how much of a wire comes back after 48 hours? Who uses the finance system that one archive could compromise?

example.learner: Worst case we lose the invoice amount, and IT deals with the rest.
example.reply: Before you hand it to IT — how much of a wire do you think comes back after the first day? And that ZIP doesn't open on IT's machine, it opens on yours. What does your login reach?

neutral.look_for: Names the direct financial loss clearly but stops there — no systemic risk.
neutral.response: Confirms the wire-loss read, then asks about the paths still unexamined — what the attachment could do, and what a skipped check teaches the office.

example.learner: If the wire goes out on a fake invoice, that money's basically unrecoverable.
example.reply: Right — the wire is the direct path. Two more to play forward: what could that ZIP do if someone opened it, and what does it teach this office if 'today, don't call' works even once?

strong.look_for: Maps all three: unrecoverable wire, malware/credential compromise through the archive, and the cultural cost of bypassed verification.
strong.response: Confirms the full map and sharpens the takeaway: the attacker is betting on speed beating process.

example.learner: The wire's unrecoverable, the ZIP could compromise my machine and our finance access, and every time someone skips verification under pressure it gets easier to skip next time.
example.reply: That's the whole board — money, machine, and habit. Notice the common thread: every path depends on speed beating process. Take the speed away and the attack has nothing.

debrief.label: The three damage paths
debrief.purpose: Names the full risk picture regardless of path.
key_points: Direct loss: a fraudulent wire is usually unrecoverable within days.
Compromise: one opened archive can expose your machine and your finance-system access.
Culture: every verification skipped under pressure trains the organization to skip the next one.
debrief.final_word: The attack needs speed to beat process. Your job is to take the speed away.

phases.label: The Response
phases.purpose: The learner commits to the concrete response sequence, in order.

practice.purpose: The learner states what they do right now — the ordered sequence, not a vibe of caution.

when.requirement: Learner commits to not interacting with the message, verifying out-of-band via a known channel, and reporting through the official channel — as concrete ordered actions.

exit.final_word: That sequence — hands off, verify out-of-band, report, preserve — is the entire job.

transition.text: That's the response. Let's lock it down, step by step.

opening_messages.text: It's 9:40 AM. The email is open in front of you and the "today" is doing its work. What exactly do you do, in order?

unthoughtful.look_for: Deletes it, ignores it, or replies to the sender to ask if it's real; may forward it to a coworker "to check."
unthoughtful.response: Stops the harmful moves first — replying and forwarding touch the attack — then rebuilds the sequence from "don't interact."

example.learner: I'd reply asking them to confirm, and CC my manager so someone else has seen it.
example.reply: Replying goes straight to the attacker — they'll happily confirm. And the CC spreads the pressure, not the safety. Start from hands-off: what channel do you have to the REAL CFO that this email didn't give you?

neutral.look_for: Doesn't interact and verifies out-of-band, but forgets to report — or reports but would delete the evidence.
neutral.response: Confirms the verification instinct, then asks what's still missing — how security learns this campaign exists, and what happens to the message itself.

example.learner: I wouldn't touch the attachment, and I'd call the CFO's office directly on the number from our directory.
example.reply: Exactly right on both — a known channel, not the one the email offered. Two questions left: how does security ever find out this campaign is running, and what happens to the email sitting in your inbox?

strong.look_for: The full ordered sequence: no interaction, out-of-band verification via a known channel, official report, evidence preserved.
strong.response: Confirms the sequence and closes the loop on why order matters — verification protects you; reporting protects everyone else.

example.learner: Don't click or reply. Call the CFO's office on the directory number to verify. Report it with the phish button. Leave the email exactly as it is for security.
example.reply: Complete, in the right order, and for the right reasons — the verification protects your ledger; the report protects the other three hundred inboxes this landed in.

interaction.input_placeholder: What do you do, in order?…

debrief.label: The response, locked
debrief.purpose: Delivers the canonical sequence and its rationale.
key_points: Do not click, open, reply, or forward — every interaction touches the attack.
Verify out-of-band through a channel you already trust — never one the message provides.
Report through the official channel so security can block and warn at scale.
Preserve the message untouched — it is evidence, not clutter.
debrief.final_word: Hands off, verify out-of-band, report, preserve. Speed is their weapon; process is yours.

component_groups.title: Recognize
components: Check the address beneath the display name — the underlying address, not the familiar name, is the identity.
Treat urgency plus isolation ("today", "don't call") as a pressure pattern, not a reason to hurry.
Treat an unexpected archive attachment as a malware vehicle until proven otherwise.
Reconcile every payment request against your own system of record.

component_groups.title: Weigh
components: A fraudulent wire is usually unrecoverable within days — the direct loss is permanent.
One opened archive can compromise your machine and your finance-system access — the attachment is a door, not a document.
Every verification skipped under pressure trains the organization to skip the next one — the habit is a target too.

component_groups.title: Respond
components: Do not click, open, reply, or forward the message.
Verify out-of-band with the claimed sender through a known, trusted channel.
Report through the official phishing-report channel immediately.
Preserve the message untouched as evidence for the security team.

ideal_response.summary: A payment request that arrives with a spoofed identity, manufactured urgency, an unexpected archive, and no matching record is a phish — and what it puts at risk is the unrecoverable wire, the compromised machine, and the habit of verification itself: touch nothing, verify out-of-band through a channel you already trust, report it officially, and preserve the evidence. The attack depends on speed beating process, and the response is to take the speed away.
